slides.4.title: Four Climate Factors That Shape a Vintage
slides.4.html:
1. 🌸 Winter and spring rainfall (soil water reserves)

Annual rainfall in the Douro averages 700-900mm, mostly in autumn and winter. A moderate amount of spring rain secures soil moisture reserves, which is key during the summer dry spell.A winter that is too dry (such as 2012) leads to excessive water stress in summer.

2. ☀️ Summer temperature and sunshine

Average summer temperatures in the Douro are 25–35°C, and July–August heat can reach 40°C+.Moderate heat promotes ripening, but extreme heatwaves (such as 2003) cause over-ripeness, a surge in sugar and loss of acidity.

3. 🌙 Diurnal temperature range

Altitude differences in the Douro (50–900m) create a marked diurnal range, and cool nights help preserve acidity and aromatic compounds. High-altitude vineyards (such as some plots in the Douro Superior) can retain fresh acidity even in warm years.

4. 🌧️ Rain during harvest (September–October)

The most critical factor: rain in the 2–3 weeks before harvest leads to:

  • Grapes absorbing water and swelling, diluting flavour
  • Outbreaks of grey rot (Botrytis)
  • Uneven ripening, forcing a rapid harvest

Conversely, a dry, cool harvest period (as in 2011, 2004 and 2000) is a common feature of top vintages.
slides.5.question: Which of the following vintages is widely regarded as one of the best of the 21st century in the Douro Valley, and was also declared by Barca Velha?
slides.5.explanation: 2004 was the peak vintage for dry Douro red, and Barca Velha was declared in that year (a very rare event). It was also a top Vintage Port year. The weather before harvest was dry, so the grapes ripened fully and kept good acidity.
